The inhabitants of this Town were aroused from their peaceful slumber at a few minutes before four þÿo clockthis morning, by the sudden and slow peals ot the Bell at l ort Christian, which was followed by the alarm Cun, thus indicating that a tire had broken out in some part ot the city. My four þÿo clock a concourse ot persons were moving towards the spot whence the lire originated, and it was soon discovered that volumes of smoke were issuing from the Apothecary Ilall, caused by the igniting ot a quantity of Phosphorus which had been put away in one of the lower stores. i\o time was lost in bringing out the different Engines; but as Providence would have it, they were not brought into active requisition, for had they been used, this would have tended to increase rather than allay the tire. The greatest alarm prevailed about this þÿtime all endeavouring to suggest the best mode of suppressing the igneous element, as it was louiul that in consequence of the smoke which prevailed, none could approach the combustible þÿmatter when at the suggestion of Mr. II. Hansen, and the unremitting perseverance and encouraging advice of one or two gentlecourse to suppress the fire was then re- men to the bystanders, the only proper sorted to, and a quantity of sand was soon in use, which had the happy effect of smothering the tire in a great degree, and ultimately causing the combustion to cease burning. Too much praise cannot be awarded to the women of the town þÿ who are always at hand at these

momentous times þÿ for their activity and usefulness on the occasion ; but we were indeed sorry to witness the apathy exhibited by some of our townsmen, who appeared to enjoy the scene, rather than afford their assistance to extinguish the devouring element. In noticing the exertions of the women, we cannot pass over the characteristic and praise-worthy zeal of the military. The soldiers deserve the gratitude of the community, ft really afforded us satisfaction þÿ in the midst of all the confusion þÿ to observe the calm, steady and persevering manner and þÿheart to work. In Central America there is reason to hope that a federal confederacy is about to be established between several States upon a model not unlike our own government, and under auspices which give hope of its maintaining a permanent existence. The basis of a confederation between Nicaragua, San Salvador, and Honduras was formed in November, 1849, and agreed to by representatives from those states, in December, 1850. A General Congress, called to meet in December next, is to complete the details of the Confederacy. These three States embrace a territory of 145,000 square miles, with a population of a little more than a million. Guatemala and Costa Rica, who have hitherto stood aloof, are invited to become members of the Confederacy. These States have a territory of 08,000 square miles, and a population of all somewhat million. If these States can be uni- more than a ted, they will possess an area of territory somewhat greater than that of France. If the town of San Juan de Nicaragua be given up by Great Britain to the State of Nicaragua, as there is reason to anticipate, the new State will have the control of the most important commercial port in the world. And even if surrendered with the guarantee of its being a free port, according to the Bulwerand Clayton treaty, the State must derive great advantage from it. þÿ Harper's Magazine for August.

By what would seem almost an oversight, the functions of the executive and j prove legislative branches of the Government at the period of the election there is j citly obey expire so nearly at the same time, that practically an interregnum. The election of the new Assembly must take place preceding the expiration of the between the 45th and the 30th day term of the present legislative body. The term of the present Assembly expires on the 28th ol May, 1852, so that the new election must occur between the 13th and the 29th of April. The term of the President ceases on the second Sunday in May, so that within a month at furtn- i is to be a þÿ Porto est, possibly within a fortnight, both branches ol the Government have to be j renewed. It is this which renders the coming election so critical. The peculiar state of the suffrage question furnishes another element of discord. The Government was elected by universal suffrage, evciy Frenchman, of the age of 21 years, being entitled to vote at j the place of his residence. But last year by the law of May 31, it was enacted that a legal residence could only be obtained by a continuous habitation of three years. It is now beyond a doubt that the labours of the members of the commission, elected for the purpose of reporting upon the draft of the Colonial Law, will shortly be brought to a close, as we understand that they are again summoned to meet at Government-House on the 12th instant, to consider the amendments that may possibly be proposed in the draft of the report, which has been drawn up by the committee, consisting of Counsellors Kunzen and Ohsten, and Lawyer N. A. Bahneberg. As the draft of the report of the Colonial Law will decidedly be passed with such amendments as may be adopted, we beg to put the members of the commission in remembrance of the necessity and ments as these, practicability of viz adopting : such amend- 1, the term of service for a member of of the Colonial Assembly not to exceed three years þÿ the half of the members to retire at a given period within the allotted time of service ; 2, the right of voting to be more generally extended; and 3, the Colonial Assembly to meet twice or thrice a year. With such and other necessary amendments as these, the draft of the Colonial Law will undoubtedly give satisfaction to the majority of the inhabitants of the danish colonies ; and we trust that the commission will consider well on the many important changes that ought to be effected in these islands þÿ changes calculated to suit local circumstances, and to ameliorate the condition of all classes.

EaP We copy the following communication from the St. Thomas Times of (lie Gth September : þÿ Communication TO TIIK EDITOR OT' TIIE TIDENDE." to Mr. Editor, þÿ please your " numerous readers" by As in your endeavours the collection of interesting and important. facts, 1 presume you are able to enlighten me as regards a report which current of the intended re-organization of the Militia, 1 beg of you to let me know if such a tiling is really the case, and at ihe same time, if with any foundation, please enlighten me with respect to The conditions can be seen at the j the utility of such a step, and of the services hitherto rendered to our town by the Militia, as I have never been abic to discover oi comprehend them. It can hardl) be with the intention of condemning to disturbance and annoyance the peaceable inhabitants in the vicinity of (be Guard House, that the re-establishment of the night watch is to take place, neither can 1 suppose the demoralizing gambling table is deemed again necessary, in order to recreate the dull hours of the night to the special injury of its visitors. Some time has elapsed since that our National Guard has done no actual service. Has there been any complaint of disorder or crime during such interregnum? 1 answer none; the town is perfectly tranquil, and to say the truth, order appears to have improved since its defenders are at rest. 1 do not apprehend that any one will refuse to join in rendering the homage due to the excellent and peaceful charac-

ter of the inhabitants of St. Thomas þÿ they have never taken part in any of the movements which have distracted the neighbouring Islands. On an apparently urgent occasion some time since, an appeal was made to the friends of order, which was responded to by all classes with a zeal of which we may proudly boast, and 1 am confident that there would he no abatement of such feeling on any future occasion under similar circumstances ; what necessity is there therefore to interrupt the present state of things, to oblige us to leave our business to play t he game of soldiers on our glorious Champ de Mars? Our fellow townsmen possess too much good sense than to imagine that a coat of any color bedecked with tawdry tinsel, and accompanying military equipments, can give them greater importance than their meritorious discharge of moral and civil duties can earn for them ; such an idea 1 am confident would he scouted by cver\ man of sense, and would leave the deluded and infatuated beings who would fain believe so glaring a folly in the situation of the Ass in the fable, who having found a Lion's skin, covered himself with it, thinking to impress on his neighbors his importance, but on attempting to roar, he unfortunately brayed, and to say (he least of it fell under the kicks of ridicule to which he had so gratui tou-dv exposed h'tnsclf. Yours, A CIVILIAN.

EDUCATION IN AMERICA. What is the enterprise and general prosperity of the Americans 1o be attributed to (their country is not naturally so rich or fruitful as Mexico), except to their general enlightenment? The oldest manufacturers of cotton in the world are the Hindoos; labor with them is cheaper than it is in any other part of the world; yet we take cotton that grows at the doors of their factories, bring it 13,(H)U miles to this country, manufacture it here where labor is so expensive, take it native and undersell the hack 13,000 miles, manufacturer. Labor is dearer in America than in any part of the world, and yet we dread and fear their competition more than that of any other nation. The reason of ail this is obvious. All the advantages which the Hindoo possesses are far more than counterbalanced by his intellectual inferiority to ourselves; while we dread the American, with reason, because lie is, intellectually at least, our equal, and, and considering telligence good conduct the general in- of the hands lie employs, our superior. To what cause, except that of a decided superiority in captains and crews, can we attribute the fact that the Americans have deprived us of so large a portion of the whale fishery, as in a measure to have monopolized it? American clocks, which wc now see in almost every hall and cottage, ought to set us thinking. We may be sure of this, the commerce of the world will fall into the hands of those who are most deserving of it. It political or philanthropic considerations

should fail to show us the necessity of educating our people, commercial considerations will one day remind us of \\ hat we ought to have done. Wc can only hope that the reminder may not come too late. Enlightenment is the great necessity and the great glory of our age; ignorance is the most expensive, and most dangerous, and most pressing of all our evils. Among ourselves we find a variety of motives converging upon this conclusion The statesman has become

aware that an enlightened population is more orderly, more submissive, in times of public distress, to the necessity of their circumstances; not so easily led away by agitators; iri short, more easily and more cheaply governed. The political economist is well aware of the close connection between general intelligence and successful enterprise and industry. The greater the number of enlightened and intelligent persons, the greater is the number of those whose thoughts are at work in subduing nature, improving arts, and increasing national wealth. The benevolent man is anxious that all should share those enjoyments and advantages which he himself finds to be the greatest, Both Churchman and Dissenter know well enough that they are under the necessity of educating. And the manufacturer, too, who is employing, perhaps, many more hands than the colonel of a regiment commands, is now becoming well aware bow much to his advantage it is that his mtn should prefer a book or a reading-room to the parlor of a public house ; should understand what they are about, instead of being merely able to go through their allotted task as so many beasts of burden ; and that they should have the strong motive of making their homes decent and respectable, and of bettering their condition. i8«ic September issi. To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Sir! 1 have noticed an extract made by you from the St. Thomas Times, and cannot perceive in what manner that publication can apply to the Militia of St. Croix. þÿ In the first place, we are not subject to such a large influx of strangers of all nations in our towns ; therefore, we have not been 111 the habit of keeping up a regular night guard, except on particular occasions, when from Ihe carefulness and attention of those in command any improper conduct resulting from ennui or in order "to recreate the dull hours of night" have been suppressed. I presume that the Authorities in St. Thomas in establishing a night guard have been actuated by the best motives from the frequency of fires, and with the view of preventing the recurrence of that awful calamity if, their good intentions have been frustrated, or that which was intended as a protection to the community has degenerated into a nuisance, the fault must lie elsewhere. That a well organized Militia should be preserved in Ibis Island, I do maintain; for during the insurrection of the negroes on the 3d of July 1848, allow me to ask who defended the town of Christiansted from pillage and fire? The Militia. M ho readily and at a moment's warning took up arms in defence of the country? The Militia. Who in a great measure suppressed the insurrectionary movement ? The Militia. In fact on all and everv occasion the Militia has ever been found able and willing to do their duty.

In hy-gone days I have played the soldier too on the " Champ de Mars," when I have always endeavoured to discharge that obligation with promptness and cheerfulness. As I think from the remarks I have made I have sufficiently proved that a well trained Militia is a valuable auxiliary force in the hands of Government, I shall pursue this subject no further. C.

a 1'lilsoa aaecdote. In tlic year 1834, a widow lady of good fortune (whom we shall call Mrs. i many Newton), resided with her daughter in one of the suburbs nearest to the metropolis. They lived in fashionable style, and kept an ample establishment of servants. A very pretty young girl, nineteen years of age, resided in this family in the capacity of lady's maid. She was tolerably educated, spoke with grammatical correctness, and was distinguished by a remarkably gentle and fascinating address. At that time Miss Newton was engaged to be married to one Captain Jennings, II. N.; and Miss Newton (as many young ladies in the like circumstances have done before), employed her leisure in embroidering cambric, making it up into handkerchiefs, and sending them and other little presents of that description, to Captain Jennings. I nhappily, but very naturally, she made Charlotte Mortlock, her maid, the bearer of these tender communications. The c iplain occupied lodgings suited to a gentleman of station, and thither ('barlotto Mortlock frequently repaired at tiie bidding of her young mistress, and generally waited (as lovers are generally impatient) to take back the captain's answers. V strange sort of regard, or attachment (it is confidently believed to have been guiltless) sprung up between the captain and the maid; and the captain, who would seem to have deserved Miss Newton's confidence as little as her maid did, gave as presents to Charlotte, some of the embroidered oiferings of .Miss

Newton. Il happened that a sudden appointment to the command of a ship of war, look Captain Jennings on a transatlantic voyage, lie had not been very long none, when the following discovery threw the family ot the Newtons into a stale of intense agitation. In search of some missing article in the absence of her maid, Miss Newton betook herself to that young woman's room, and. quite unsuspiciously, opened a trunk which was left unlocked. There site found, to her horror, a number ot the handkerchiefs she had embroidered for her lover. The possibility of the real truth never flashed across her mind; the dishonesty of Charlotte seemed to lie the only solution of the incident. þÿ " Doubtless," she reasoned, " the pareels had been opened on their way to Captain Jennings, and their stolen." On the return of Charlotte Mortlock, she was charged with the robbery. þÿ What availed the assertion that she had received the handkerchiefs lroni the captain himself? It was no defence, second messenger was and certainly was not calculated to soften the anger of her mistress. A policeman was summoned, the unhappy girl was charged with felony, underwent cxami nation, was committed for trial, and, destitute of witnesses, or of any proba- 1 ble defence, was ultimately convic "

N 0 I ATI! a» The judge (now deceased) who tried the case, was unsparingly denounced by philanthropic ladies, for the admiration he had expressed for the weeping girl, and especially lor his announcement one year's imprisonment with hard labor, ' that lie would not transport her, since j and her health had been well sustained. the country could not afford to loose such beauty." It was doubtless, not a very judicial remark ; hut an innocent girl was, at all events, saved lrom a sentence that might have killed her. Consigned to tiie Countv House of Correction, Charlotte Mortlock observed the best possible conduct þÿ was modest, bumble, submissive, and industrious þÿ and soon gained the good-will of all her supervisors. To the governor she always asserted her innocence, and told, with great simplicity, the tale of her fatal possession of those dangerous gilts. She had been in prison a few months, when the governor received a visit from a certain old baronet, who with ill-disguised reluctance, and in the blunt phraseology which was peculiar to him, proceeded to say, that "A girl named lotte Mortlock! Charlotte Mortlock had quite bewitched his friend Captain Jennings, who was j beyond the Atlantic ; and that a letter he produced would show the singular | altogether she looked frame of mind in which the captain was, about that girl." Assuredly, the letter teemed with expressions of anguish, remorse, and horror at the suffering and apparent ruin of " a dear innocent girl," the victim of his

senseless and heartless imprudence. þÿ However, the baronet seemed to he any thing hut touched by bis friend's rhapsodies. He talked much of "human nature," and of "the weakness ot a man ' when a pretty girl was in the ease;" but, in order to satisfy bis friend's mind, asked to see her, that he might write some account of her appearance and condition. Accordingly, he did sec her, in the governor's presence. After a few inappropriate questions, he cut the interview short, and went away, manifestly disposed to account his gallant friend a fool for his excitement. The incident was not lost upon the governor, who listened with increased faith to the poor girl's protestations. In a few months more he received a stronger confirmation of them. Apparently unsatisfied with the baronet's service, Captain Jennings wrote to another triend ot his, a public functionary, formerly a captain in the renowned Light Division ; and that officer placed in the governor's contents | hand a letter from the captain, expressfate of an innocent young woman. ing unbounded grief for the dreadlul " He could not rest night or day ; she haunted his imagination, and yet he was distant, and powerless to serve her." His touched with pity, and consulted the governor as to the proper steps to pursue. However, under the unhappy circumstances oi the case, Captain Jennings being so tar away, no formal document being at hand, and the period of the poor girl's release being then almost come, it was (Teemed

inadvisable to take any step. Charlotte dortlock fulfilled the judgment of the aw. She had been carefully observed, her occupation had been of a womanly charto the jury, in passing sentence of j acter ; she hail never incurred a reproof, much less a punishment, in the prison ;

Slie, consequently, quitted her sail abode in a condition suitable for active exertion. Such assistance as could he extended to her, on her departure, was afforded, and so she was launched into the wide world of London. She soon found herself penniless. þÿ Happily, she did not linger in want, paw u her clothes (which were gooil), and gradually descend to the extreme privation which has assailed so many similarly circumstanced. She resolved to act, and again went to the prison gates. Well attired, but deeply vailed, so as to defy recognition, she inquired for the governor. The gate porter announced that "a lady" desired to speak to him. The stranger was shown in, the vail was uplifted, and, to the governor's astonishment, there stood Char- Her hair was neatly and becomingly arranged about her face; her dress was quiet and pretty ; and so young, so lovely, and, at the same time, so modest and innocent, that the governor, perforce, almost excused the inconstancy (albeit attended with such fatal consequences) of Captain Jennings. With many tears she acknowledged her grateful obligations for the considerate and humane treatment she had received in prison. She disclosed her poverty, and her utter friendlessness ; expressed her horror of the temptations to which she was exposed ; and implored the govcrror's counsel and assistance. Without a moment's hesitation, she was advised to go at once to a lady of station, whose extensive charities and zealous services, rendered to the out-

casts of society at that time, were most remarkable. She cheerfully acquiesced. She found the good lady at home, related her history, met with sympathy and active aid, and, after remaining for a time, by her benevolent recommendation, in a charitable establishment, was recommended to a wealthy family, to whom every particular of her history was confided. In this service she acquitted herself with perfect trustfulness and fidelity, and won her warmest regard. The incident which had led to her unmerited imprisonment, broke oil the engagement between Captain Jennings and Miss Newton; but whether the former had ever an opportunity of indemnifying I lie poor girl for the suffering she had undergone, the narrator has never been able 1o learn. This is, in every particular, a true case of prison experience. þÿ Harper's Magazine.

THE EDIBLE BIRDS' NESTS OF CHINA. Ymong the various articles exposed tor sale to the natives, in the innumerable streets of Canton, the edible birds'-nests deserve especial notice. They owje their celebrity only to the whimsical luxury of the Chinese, and arc brought principally from Java and Sumatra, though they are found on most of the rocky inlets of the Indian Archipelago. The nest is the habitation of a small swallow, named (from the circumstance of having an edible house) liirundo escidenta. They arc composed of a mucilaginous substance, but as yet have never been analyzed with sufficient accuracy to show the constituents. Externally, they resemble t ll-concocted, fibrous isinglass, and are of a white color, inclining to red. Their thickness is little more than that of a silver spoon, and the weight from a quarter to half an ounce. When dry, they arc brittle, and wrinkled ; the size is nearly that of a goose's egg. Those that are dry, white, and clean, are the most valuable. They are packed in bundles, with split rattans run through them to preserve the shape. Those procured after the young are fledged are'iiot salable in China. The quality of the nests, varies according to the situation and extent of the caves, and the time at which they are taken. If procured before the young are fledged, the nests arc of the best kind ; if they contain eggs only, they ire still valuable ; but, if the young are m the nests, or have left them, the whole arc then nearly worthless, being dark-

colored, streaked with blood, and intermixed with feathers and dirt. These nests are procurable twice everv year; the best arc found in deep, damp caves, which, if not injured, will continue to produce indefinitely. It was once thought that the caves near the sea-coast were the most productive ; but some of the most profitable yet found, are situated fitly miles in the interior. This fact seems to be against the opinion, that the nests arc composed of the spawn offish, or of bcclie-de-mer. The method of procuring these nests is not unattended with danger. Some of the caves are so precipitous, that no one, but those accustomed to the employment from their youth, can obtain the nests, being only approachable by a perpendicular descent of many hundred feet, by ladders of bamboo and rattan, over a sea rolling violently against the rocks. When the mouth of the cave is attained, the perilous task of taking the nests must often he performed by torchlight, by penetrating into recesses of the rock, where the slightest slip would be instantly fatal to the adventurers, who see nothing below them but the turbulent surf, making its way into the chasms of the rock þÿ such is the price paid to gratify luxury. After the nests are obtained, they are separated from feathers and dirt, arc carefully dried and packed, and are then fit, for the market. The Chinese, who

<X» ATI are the only people that purchase them for their own use, bring them in junks to this market, where they command extravagant prices ; the best, or white kind, often being worth four thousand dollars per pecul, which is nearly twice their weight in silver. The middling kind is worth from twelve to eighteen hundred, and the worst, or those procured after fledging, one hundred and fifty to two hundred dollars per pccul. The majority of the best kind are sent to Pekin, for the use of the court. It appears, therefore, that this curious dish is only an article of expensive luxury among the Chinese. The Japanese do not use it at all, and how the former people acquired the habit of indulging in it, is only less singular than their persevering in it. They consider the edible bird's-ncst as a great stimulent, tonic, and aphrodisiac, but its best quality, perhaps, is its being perfectly harmless. The labor bestowed to render it fit for the table is enormous : every feather, stick, or impurity of any kind, is carefully removed: and then, alter undergoing many washings and preparations, it is made into a soft, delicious jelly. The sale of birds'nests is a monopoly with all the governments in whose dominions they are found. About two hundred and fifty thousand pcculs, at a value of one million four hundred thousand dollars, are annually brought to Canton. These come from the islands of Java, Sumatra. Macassar, and those of the Soolno group. Java alone sends about thirty thousand

pounds, mostly of the first quality, estimated at seventy thousand dollars. I am indebted for much information on this curious article of commerce, to the captain of a Java ship, a very well informed man, trading regularly to China, who had large quantities on board, and whose wife, a native of that country, to satisfy niv curiosity, prepared a dinner for me of Chinese dishes, including the bird's-ncst and the sea-slug, both of which I partook of, and found them very palatable. þÿ BtrncaitlCs Voyage to China.

A r a meeting of Clerks, held by special appointment, at the Merchants Exchange, in Buck Island, Sir GIEl.OT was called to the Chair. The Chairman opened the meeting, and in a brief manner impressed oil the numerous audience present the necessity of an energetic appeal to the community in behalf of the respectable body ot Clerks, who, notwithstanding the heat of the weather, their multitudinous writings at this season, and the extra number of Accounts Current which fall under their supervision, are called upon to make out duplicates and triplicates ot Accounts, which have been already delivered to, and mislaid by, the Debtors þÿ proposed the following Resolutions, w hich were carried item ran. item! ved, þÿ That while the making out of an original gives pleasure, that ot making out duplicates and triplicates is vexatious, annoying, and everything but pleasant. I Iandeed. þÿ That those whose duty it falls to, to make repeated calls, in the hot sunshine, are entitled to commisscration, and ought to be relieved lrom heated appeals to the cool debtors. Resolved. þÿ That with a view to alleviate the preceding grievances, they pledge themselves to send and pay every account they owe, and hold it as unjust in every one who refuses to act up to the principle of rendering unto Caesar, the tilings that are Ca-sar's." Resolved. þÿ That the foregoing Resolutions he published in the Gazettes ot the neighbouring Islands. The meeting, after a vote of thanks to the Chairman, adjourned.

Ah American Editress writes thus boldly ol marriage : þÿ " Many arc of opinion t hat, if it were not for stringency of the civil law,, nearly all the families would he broken up, and society go into chaos. We have no such notion. If a proclamation were made to-day, declaring every marriage in the union null and void, and leaving it once more to the choice of the parties whether the relation he renewed, business would he suspended, newspapers would slop, stores, factories, and workshops, would close. DIRECT STEAM COMM1 NICATION FROM GENOA TO NEW YORK. We extract the following from the letter of our correspondent at Genoa, dated July 21: þÿ "A new line of steam communication, direct from Genoa to New 4 ork, has been organised by Messrs. 1. Kingston, Wells &. Co., of that city. Mr. Roster, a gentleman interested in the undertaking, and from whom I have received an account of the project, is staying in Piedmont, in order to prepare the necessary steps for coming to an agreement with the Sardinian Government with regard to the mails. I am happy to say that Count favour, to whom as Minister of Commerce, the plan has been submitted, has given the sanction of the Government. A grant has been made to the company for the exclusive working of this line for fifteen years, the annual sum of S 50,000 being guaranteed for the transport of the mails. These steamers will touch at Madeira, where letters or passengers will be transferred to the South American line of steamers, so that it may be looked upon as a double line both to the south and north of the American continent. The agreement entered into with the Government of this country is very fair, all port charges and duties being free. The company arc also in treaty with the Portuguese and South American Governments for the transport of their mails, and arc likely to be successful in obtaining them on favourable conditions. I am informed that the Government, as is its

3 T (0 'Ji © 1 ATI 3-. custom, has endeavoured to facilitate this as much as possible, consistent v. itli its wish to encourage a liberal spirit of enterprise, and to enlarge the trade with America. According to statistical returns, the importation of cotton to thi port during last year amounted to fifteen millions of francs ; a direct steam communication will not fail to increase this amount, which was entirely for home consumption. When the railway to Switzerland is completed, no doubt can be entertained that Genoa will, by its medium, largely supply that manufacturing country with its raw material, which at the present moment it draws from other ports, chiefly Havre. The export trade in fruits from the Mediterranean to America is calculated at sixty millions per annum. A cargo of fresh fruits generally loses three-fourths m ils value during its passage, as sailing vessels must on an average lie reckoned to require a three months' journey. These steamers may be expected to clear the distance in about sixteen days, and, time being a prime consideration with so dainty a cargo, a full supply ol the article may fairly be reckoned upon. The tide of emigration from Germany andt-v.itzerlanil lias, at present, as no direct communication exists from the Mediterranean to Niw York, to take its way either to some part ol North Germany or of England ; but, as soon as these steamers begin to ply, a shorter, quicker, and consequently much cheaper, route will be opened for it. These considerations
speak most certainly in favor of the project, which is the beginning of a new era in the commercial connexion of the Mediterranean with America." þÿ Morning Chronicle.

Brother Jonathan.- The origin of þÿ this term, as applied to the United States, is given in a recent number of The Norwich Courier. That Editor says it was communicated by a gentleman now upwards of eighty years of age, who was an active participator in the scenes of the revolution. The story is as follows : þÿ " When General Washington, being appointed commander of the army of the revolutionary war, came to Massachusetts to organise it, and make preparations for the defence of the country, he found great want of ammunition and a other means necessary to meet the powerful foe he had to contend with, and great difficulty to obtain them. If attacked in such condition, the cause at once might he hopeless. On one occasion, at that anxious period, a consultation of the officers and others was had, when it seemed no way could be devised to make such preparations as were necessary. His Excellency, Jonathan Trumbull, the elder, was then Governor of the State of Connecticut, on whose judgment and aid the General placed the greatest reliance, and remarked, ' We must consult Brother Jonathan on the subject.' The General did so, and the Governor was successful in supply- ing many of the wants of the army. þÿ Bridge, When difficulties afterwards arose, and 'lie army was spread over the country, it became a bv-word, We must consult ' Brother Jonathan.' The term Yankee is still applied to a portion, but Bro- 1 ther Jonathan' has now become a designation of the whole country, as John
Bull has for England." þÿ (Dictionary of Americanisms, bv John Russell Bartlett, 1 8 If).) þÿ From A ofes anil Queries.

Sculpture n\ an Irisii Lady. þÿ A remarkable piece of sculpture, the production of a Dublin lady, has lately been placed in the Great Exhibition. The Times recently referred to it in terms of marked admiration, and expressed its regret that it had not been forwarded earlier, so that all the visiters of the Exhibition might have partaken in a gratification that must now be enjoyed by a greatly diminished number. The London correspondent of Saunders gives the following account of this beautiful production: þÿ " London , Saturday. þÿ On revisiting the Exhibition, yesterday, my attention was attracted to an additional contribution from Ireland, which tinds an appropriate place in the British avenue, not far from the great crystal fountain. It is a large glass case, containing a block of marble, sculptured by Miss Kennedy of Merrion-square, Dublin, the subject being 'A Scene at a Northern Irish Fair,' the actors in which, thirtyone in number, are pourtrayed in relief. Of its merits as a work of art, I cannot

A T I write too highly. The figures are so artistically grouped, and the attitudes so judiciously developed, that there is a total absence of that confusion which so frequently mars the finest effect of the chisel of artist or amateur. ' The Scene' is well conceived, and boldly executed ; and whether we study the principal group of six rollicking Irish boys, and their partners, in undisturbed possession of ' the dure' þÿ the fiddlers who produce the harmony þÿ or the old woman, so charmed by it that she, too, is ' footing it' as well as her old limbs will allow þÿ the group at the side driving bargain a for some meal þÿ or the less prominent figures, we find a perfect and finished realization in stone of the peculiar characteristics of the Irish character, the more perfect because it partakes not of exaggerated caricature. As a work ot art, it can bear comparison with much of the sculpture in the Exhibition ; and Miss Kennedy has every reason to be proud of having put forward this additional proof of her country's talent before the Congress of All Nations. Placed in a good position, it is not passed over, and elicits so much admiration, that it is to be regretted it was not placed in the Exhibition sooner. It has been sent over at the express wish of the gentlemen who composed the Committee of Management lbr the Exhibition in Dublin."

at þÿ 25, 508. Fire-proof Bank, San Francisco. þÿ We find, in the San Francisco Herald, a | long account of .Messrs. þÿAdams slire- j proof banking-house, just erected. Ac- j cording to this, in the centre oi the mas- 1 j sive walls, and pervading throughout their whole extent, is a vacant space, 1 four inches wide, communicating with the air through sieve-like apertures in the cellar and the parapet. The floor of the basement and of the small yard in the rear is a solid coat ot cement, several inches thick. Beneath the surface of the yard is a reservoir, containing several thousand gallons of water, from

which a pipe leads underground into the basement, where a force pump is attached. A hose leads from thence up through all the floors to the roof, it ne- j cessary. In a back corner of the room is the vault, and here all the resources of art have been exhausted to make assurance doubly sure. This vault rests upon a solid foundation of brickwork, extending below to the floor of the cellar. The floor is a mosaic pavement, forced of diamond-shaped stones, alternately white and slate-coloured. þÿ On the roofþÿ the point usually most exposed in case of fire, the utmost care has been bestowed to render it proot against the attacks of the most tierce heat. A parapet wall, two feet thick and six feet high, extends around and above. The roof is first covered with vine, soldered so as to be air-tight; upon that rests a bed of cement, one inch thick, and upon that again is a pavement of fire-proof tiles, laid in cement, and air-tight. The doors and windows are furnished, at top and bottom, with thick plates of cast-iron, one yard wide, and embedded in the masonry. The sides arc double frames of iron, two feet apart, with brickwork intervening. The doors and shutters arc double, with the same interval of two feet between. They are constructed of boiler-iron, an eighth of an inch thick, and braced in every direction with iron bar# an inchf þÿthick.

A double and fearful crime lias been committed by an unhappy individual, whom the criminal defection oi bis wife bad plunged into a state of despair, by which, doubtless, his reason was affected. M. Sellerier, an extensive silver-smith, had been, for fourteen ve.irs, married to a woman, whom lie had espoused without a fortune, but whom he found happily adapted to the requirements of a business, which, thanks to his own ability, industry, and excellent conduct, had proved completely successful. Their union had been without issue for the first ten years ; but, at length, in 1847, a fine little girl was born. Two years later, in July, 1819, a second infant, likewise a female, increased the family of the silversmith ; and for this, as of the former, Mr. C , the partner in trade of M. Sellerier, stood godfather. Two months ago, again, ' another child was born, whom the o father hailed with joy as a son. Early last week, the wife and the partner ol M. Sellerier suddenly disappeared from his residence, taking with them, in their flight, the last-born infant. Then disappearance was a thunder-stroke to the bereaved husband. Confiding, even to blindness, in bis wife, he had never entertained the least suspicion of her lideliiv ; his grief and astonishment, then, may well he guessed, when he learned that for the last eleven years the intimacy of his faithless partner with M. C was a known fart þÿ one, indeed, which

had acquired pnhlie. notoriety. At first, the unhappy man seemed weighed down with sorrow and disappointment ; but, b\ degrees, he appeared to resume courage. He redoubled bis tenderness to the two little forsaken babes, loaded them with caresses, and seemed, by concentrating' ori them all his affections, to gain an oblivion of their mother's odious abandonment. Last Saturday, M. $ went out early, and remained absent till evening. On his arrival, he shewed himself more tenderly affectionate than ever to the children, with whom he took supper, doing his best to divert them, and making them sing the songs which their mother was accustomed to teach them. Bedtime canic ; lie made them say their prayers, and placed them to sleep, each in its own cradle. He afterwards undressed, and commenced walking noiselessly to and fro in the chamber, appearing, as a neighbour deposed, 41 plunged in gloomy reflection." Yesterday (Sunday) the porter and the grant, neighbours were surprised to sec neither the children nor M. S. make their appearance. The morning passed by without either the doors or windows of his lodgings being opened ; whereupon the Police Commissairc ot the Faubourg Montmartre was advised of the fact and, he, at three o'clock in I lie afternoon, caused the doors to be opened. The small chamber, in v\ Inch the two children lay, was found inundated with blood. þÿ The two hapless little ones were found lying in their cradles, their heads sepa-

3 T o <0 © 1 A T 1 S5' rated from their bodies; whilst the lifeless body of the wretched father was found extended on the floor, the arteries of the throat divided, and still holding in his hand the razor with which he had committed the double murder and the suicide. The news of the tragic event, which rapidly spread through the neighbourhood, excited feelings of alright and pity, which it would be difficult to describe, and which were fnanifested in the crowds which for two days surrounded the theatre of this lamentable catastrophe. þÿ Gazelle des Tribunaux.

The receipts lor the day were 2,707/. 17s. þÿ Among the visiters on Monday, was M. Angelo Lusvergh, connected with the Observatory at Home, who, with ai. intelligent assistant, has been charged b\ his Holiness to visit the Exhibition, for the purpose of examining the mathematical and philosophical instruments, to getlier with the machinery in the English department. The expenses of the visit are defrayed hv his Holiness. þÿ Among the numerous collections of products at the Great Exhibition, there arc few more interesting than the curious collection of teas in the China division. Every kind of tea that is calculated to illustrate any particular manufacture or growth has here its specimen þÿ from 44 the finest flowery Pekoe that was sent to Canton for the use of a Mandarin," and which was there purchased at the rate of 50s. per pound, to different specimens of what is termed 44 Lie Tea," which is, in fact, nothing more than dust, manufactured by the Chinese, to represent the finest kinds, whilst, in fact, the spurious mixture does not contain one hit of true tea in the whole sample. We were much amused, on inspecting many different samples of physic teas þÿ or teav

made up, with and without herbs and drugs into cakes and other shapes, and used by the Chinese as medicine. One specimen hears an inscription in Chinese, stating that it 44 dissolves a glutinous spittle, dispels lniskincss, clears the mind, brightens the vision, engenders a wholesome moisture in the mouth, and moistens the lungs ; its odour is fraits taste savoury;" whilst another 44 is powerful in removing all kinds ot inflammatory diseases, as, also, those arising from the impeded circulation of the fluids ;" a third is recommended for 44 cooling the Mood;" and a fourth, like soda-water, among the barbarians, is recommended to he taken by the Celestials after too large an allowance of Sham-shoo. One cup of this mixture is stated to be "sufficient to remove any ill effects of the previous night's debauch." A specimen, marked No. 4, obtained from " the Dragon's Cavern,"

is recommended as "invaluable in quiet ing troubled feelings, in assuaging thirst, removing undigested food, dissolving phlegm, enlivening spirits" þÿ in short, for removing every ill which flesh is lieit to. In the collection there are, also, specimens of tea-flower dried. They resemble very much the ordinary camomile flowers. There are, also, seeds ot the tea plant, and some samples of remarkably fine tea that cannot be purchased, and which is said to be grown by Priests on some of the beautiful hills of I'okien. <D Q £ A T U < ev « A portion of llie commercial community in this Island held a meeting a short time ago for the purpose of discussing the propriety of establishing a steam communication between St. Thomas and St. Croix. The measure at the time met with many warm supporters, who succeeded in drawing over to their views | many more, and to a certain extent, it might have been said, a Company was formed to carry out the project ; but like many other projects raised in St. Thomas, when the time came to arrange details, opinions were so conilicting as to paralyse all progress in the matter. One of ; the points on which the greatest diversity of opinion prevailed, was to decide whether a paddle-wheel or a screw-propeller boat would answer best. That point, however, ought not to have been the one to prevent so useful an acquisition to the transit of the two Islands, as we believe it yet remains a point in dispute among scientific men which of the two inventions is the better. The þÿ nail should have been struck when þÿhot, and the inhabitants of both Islands would , have been the gainers. freight passing between this and the sister Colony, in consequence of the daily intercourse. Again, the great increase of travelling which there would natural-

he raised for the benefit of encouraging steam communication, by introducing a small local postage on letters between the Islands. In a report to the Secretary of War by Lieutenant-Colonel Jebb, the Inspector- General of Military Prisons, which lias just been printed in a Parliamentary paper, the subject of flogging in the Army is brought forward. It seems that imprisonment in lieu ofcorporal punishment has been beneficial in its operation, notwithstanding the contrary opinion expressed by military officers. Colonel Jebb states : þÿ þÿ If the views of the more experienced officers of Her þÿMajesty ser s vice as to the deterring influence of cotporal punishment were correct, a great increase of crime in the Army might have been anticipated as the necessary consequence of limiting the power of Courts-martial, and materially diminishing a mode of punishment deemed to be the most efficacious for the maintenance Capting, as he leaned on the darkey for of discipline. Sen amyl, the Prophet of the Caucasus, through whose inspiriting leadership the Caucasians have maintained a successful struggle against the gigantic power of Russia for many years, is described by a recent writer as a man of middle stature; helms light hair, gray eyes, shaded by bushy and well-arched eyebrows ; a nose finely moulded, and a small mouth. His features are distinguished from those of his race by a peculiar fairness of complexion and deliþÿ cacy of skin : the elegant form of his hands and feet is not less remarkable. The apparent stiffness ofliis arms, when he walks, is a sign of his stern and impenetrable character. His address is thoroughly noble and dignified Ofliim-

self he is completely master ; and he exerts a tacit supremacy over all who approach him. An immovable, stony calmness, which never forsakes him, even in moments of the utmost danger, broods over his countenance. He passes a sentence of death with the same com posure with which he distributes þÿ the sabre of þÿhonor to bis bravest Murids, after a bloody encounter. With traitors or criminals whom lie lias resolved to destroy he will converse w ithout betraying the least sign of anger or vengeance. He regards himself us a mere instrument in the hands of a higher Being; and holds, according to the Sufi doctrine, that all ins thoughts and determinations are immediate inspirations from God The flow of his speech is as animating and irresisthle as his outward appear ance is awful and commanding. þÿ He shoots flames from his eyes, and scatters flowers from bis þÿlips, said Bcrsek Bey, who sheltered him for some dat s after the tall of Aehulgo, when Schamyl dwelt for some time among the princes of the Djighetes and Thirties, for the purpose of inciting the tribes on the Black 8er; to rise against the Russians. Schanry! is now fifty years old, but still full of vigor and strength ; it is however said, that he has for some years past suffered from an obstinate disease of the eyes, which is constantly growing worse. He fills the intervals of leisure which his public charges allow him, in reading the Koran, fasting, and prayer. Of late vears lie has but seldom, and then only on critical occasions, taken a personal

share in warlike encounters. In spite of iiis almost supernatural activity, Scliamyl is excessively severe and temperate in his habits. A few hours ot sleep are enough for him ; at times lie will watch for the whole night, withoutshowing the least trace of fatigue on the following day. He eats little, and watei is his only beverage. According to Mohammedan custom, lie keeps sever; wives. In 1844 he had three, of which his favorite (Pearl of the Harem, as she was called) was an Armenian, of exqni site beauty.

Water Ballasting for Ships Some time since Dr. David Blair White, of Newcastle-upon-Tyne, patented apian for ballasting ships by means of water, and the patentee states that the whole arrangement is in such an advanced state, and its decided advantages over other kinds of ballast so apparent, that the apparatus will be shortly ready for application to any vessels whose owners may be desirous of availing themselves of it. The coal brig Benton, Capt. Blackett, 250 tons, which has long been fitted with the apparatus, has completely established the economy, safety, and efficiency, in every point, of this mode of ballasting. On her last arrival in the Thames, and after discharging her cargo, her crew commenced at seven þÿo clock on Thursmorning last to fill the ballast bags, which will hold sixty-seven tons of water. In forty minutes the necessary quantity was stowed away, and with the tide she sailed down the river on her passage to Sunderland for another cargo. Between sixty and seventy visitors witnessed the operation, which was highly satisfactory.

Christ landed, Monday the 21th Oct., 1851. þÿ-tl Ovfc'- The Hurricane Reason being now terminated, w e beg leave to offer a few remarks, as to I he manner in which the commencement and conclusion ot tins Season was observed here, during this year. The J5th of July last, the commencement of the Hurricane Season, was, as usual, announced the evening before, by the ringing of the bell attached to the danish church and thus proclaimed a lloly Day. This day, as well as the goth of October, have always, from time immemorial, been observed here by the þÿtown people s : but on tins Iasi occa siori, the goth of October was not formally proclaimed a Holy Day ; the town however, abstained from peop! ii - þÿwork the public offices and stores were all closed, and in most of the churches Divine Service was held. The reason why these two days are not observed by the Country People is grounded only on an old custom, as we suppose ; for, il is a well-known fact, that in the days of Slavery, the country folks did not enjoy equally will the þÿtown people, s all the Holy Days observed in the Island. The. commencement of the Season, the 25th ot July is usually set apart, as a day of Public Worship, to implore the Mercy of Almightv Cod, on entering upon such a dangerous season of the year ; and also, to beg Ills preservation from the calamities to which we are exposed. This is well and in harmony with the dictates of Reason and Religion. But why the termination of this same season should not.

be observed in a similar mannei is a piece of philosophy, which we confess we do not understand. If in the dispensation of God's providence, He spoke in anger from the clouds, and visited us with destruction both as to life and properly þÿ every heart would quake, and c\ en in the very streets men would not be ashamed to bow down and cry out for mercy; why then the danger being removed þÿ should we he less grateful? As to whether the country people would abuse these two Holy Days, we shall not attempt to give our opinion ; but leave the matter to better judges. This, however, we would say, that if they abuse them, 'it is not our fault þÿ let us, at least, set them a good example, and þÿ Render to Caesar the things that are þÿCaesar s, and to God the things that are þÿGod s. The abuse of any of þÿGod s favours is no reason, surely, why we should discontinue to use them ; were it so þÿ what is there in the world that would not fall into disuse? Wo think those days should be most solemnly and religiously observed it is a dangerous experiment to measure points with Un- Lon!. We hope that the next Hnrrieain Season will ho better observed. þÿ The Lord is very liberal, and lie never will allow men to outdo Him in generosity.

T he arrival last night of the Medway, from Chagres, furnishes ns with the important account of a most disastrous conflict between the American and Native boatmen on the Chagres Kiver. As our information is from an undoubted source, accompanied by documents below (which prove of how serious a nature was the fight þÿ approaching to civil war), vve have delayed the issue of our sheet in order to place the facts before our raiders. Captain Symons, of the Medway, has witltout doubt rendered invaluable service to the cause of order in this instance, and been the means of saving many innocent lives, and protecting valuable property from total loss W e trust we may be pardoned by that gentleman if we have incurred his displeasure by making known in this public j manner the services afforded by him during a time when nothing but barbarity, and the most blood-thirsty passions, actuated the Natives and Americans, as they stood arrayed on both sides the river, resolved to avenge themselves in each others blood. The facts arc these: the Americans who have gone to Chagres, inhabit one of the banks of the river, which is now technically called American þÿtown, ; 0f these a large number are boatmen, who are anxious to monopolize the trade of the river, and to maintain a high price (sny ®2 n passenger) for all persons going to or from the steamers. The Natives have been content with a lesser sum (SI), and hence has arisen the jealousy and ultimate consequences. On the morning of the 2lth (Octr.), after a terrible fight of

the previous day, Capt. Symons landed on the þÿNatives side, when he found the wholo population in a most violent and excited rage, bent upon going over to the þÿAmericans side, to have a thorough fight. Capt. S. here enquired if there was a leader to the mob to whom he could address himself, and | was answered no, that all felt alike determined logo; he then begged to be permitted to see if the matter could not in an amicable way be settled, so ns to avoid the evils consequent on such a stale of things. After considerable delay, Capt. S. succeeded in obtaining consent to be allowed to proceed across the river, and ascertain the views of of the opposite party. Here lie found the Americans equally infuriated and irrcconþÿc.lahie evading all the admonitions of the C S. Consul, and declaring they would go

across and (ire the town of the natives, a similar threat which Capt. Symons had heard the natives declare they would do to the Americans. At this juncture the natives had rigged a Brass Cannon on the old Fortress, and stood by with a lighted torch, with every preparation to fire; Capt. S. here waved his hand and motioned to them to desist, which they did. An eve witness asserts having seen one American lying at the Consul's door, on whose body twenty three bullet wounds were visible. At the same gentleþÿman s house lay tiie U S. mails and specie packages for the Cherokee, in the most imminent danger of being forcibly taken nwav by the mob, and which Capt. S. after a great deal of trouble succeeded in taking to his boat, and afterwards delivered on I board to the Commander ol said vessel. The .infusion and excitement which prevailed duiing the period of the outbreak made it difficult to ascertain the number of killed and wounded; they were however considerable, and it was believed equal on either side. In our desire to hasten the issue of our paper it is not improbable that we have passed over many interesting particulars which were relaled to us this morning by our informant. The documents we publish will serve to give our readers an idea of the perilous slate in which all respectable Amo ricans then in Cliagres were placed, and i only escaped with life through the humane and resolute conduct of the Commander of | the Medway. The document shewing the conditions of a truce entered into by the hos-

tile parties will prove ihat Captain Symons did not fail to bring about a temporary ces salion of hostilities. An opinion however prevailed that this would not be lasting, and that the extreme uncertainty for the protec tiou of life and property in that quarter would cause both the English and American gov crnmcnls to dispatch thither some vessels uf war. Narciso Lopez, who was publicly executed at the city of Ilavannah, on the morning of the 1st of September, was heie in Venezuela, in the year 1738, or 1799, and was, accordingly, about fifty-two years of age. ! 1 1 is father was a wealthy landed proprietor, owning large estates on the llanos or plains, swarming with cattle, horses, &c. His inoihcr, who is still living, is said to be a woman of rare moral dignity, combined wiih mental strength. Her children, imbued | with that noblest inheritance of nature, are stamped from the outset as bom to command. Narciso was the only son that lived beyond childhood, though of daughters his parents had some fourteen or fifteen ; and, according to the habitual life of the llanos, he passed almost from the cradle to the saddle. or further, we may, perhaps, say, to the back of a wild horse without any þÿsaddle a training well calculated to lay the foundation of that character and habit of fearless hardihood, energy, and resolution which has been illustrated hv his subsequent military career. Though so successful as a soldier, and though that success was achieved only by the display of extraordinary capacity as well

ST, <0 % at a as courage, it is singular that Lopez was never fond of a military profession and life. He did not enter it from choice, but simply as a resource of desperation, under circumstances forced upon him, at the age of fifteen, by the civil war then desolating all the Spanish South American provinces. His father had been stripped of nearly all his property, or had seen it rendered wholly unproductive, through the operation of that cause; and with such means as lie was able to realise, he entered into commercial life at Caracas, assisted by his son. wtio, boy as he was, was able to bear tiie burden ol a large share ol its lespousibiliiies. At the (own of Valencia, in the interior, he had the charge of a branch ol his þÿfatliei main s establishment at Caracas, at the period ol the sanguinary, and, for the time, decisive buttle ol I. a Puerta, in 1814, in which Bolivar, at the head ol the insurgent troops, was defeated by the Spanish army, under General Bows. Bolivar, though routed, sent orders to the garrison of Valencia to maintain tiie place, which was done with heroism to the lust moment, so long as lesistance was possible þÿ the inhabitants, who knew that massacre and plunder would immediately ensue, on the entrance of the victorious army, uniting in the defence with the few soldiers of the garrison. Lopez assisted himself bravely m the defence, though a mere boy. But no assistance coming from Bolivar, lliu town, alter a protracted defence, suriendered, indignant at what they considered ihe

desertion ol their chief. Alter this, chiefly ihiough penury, and partly ttirough resentment against Bolivar, he volunteered into the Spanish army, and, ere the close of the war, had reached the rank ol Colonel. Besides oilier distinctions, he received, during ilns war, the rare miliiaiy honour of the cross of San Fernando, of the second (the must disiinguished) degree, a reward not bestowed at pleasure, but winch is to be obtained only by a public demand by the pei son claiming it, and, un the institution of j a formal piocess for and against his right, i j everybody being fiee to interpose an objec- j | lion, or to depreciate the merit of the act for which it is demanded. In Die whole uimy lliograpliieal Sketch of Narciso I there was but one other individual who pos- j sessod Hus cross Lopez, not attaching such importance to the act for which he w as urged to apply, and caring little, moreover, lor the j honour himself, was only induced lo demand it by the Communder-in-Chief General Mo- 1 1 1 lo, who taunted him wiih being afraid of a rejection of the demand, and who demanded ins Secretary to diaw up the application, almost forcing the reluctant young officer to sign it. The occasion on winch he received the cross of San Fernando, was as follows : þÿ Morillo, at the head of a force ol seven or eight thousand men, was pursuing the patriot army of Paez, numbering about 3,090, over tho llanos or plains ol Venezuela, trying in vain to bring the matter to an engagement. This the latter hud, uf

course, no dilliculiy to avoid, Ins whole force consisting of lirst-rate cavalry, while the Spanish army was mainly infantry. þÿ Lopez was, at this period, as has been above mentioned, at the head of a picked squadron, reserved for a decisive moment, with which it was a point of honour never to turn their hacks. Ho had lost half of it in severe enengagement that morning, and with the rest, thirty-eight in number, was marching on the j extreme flank of the army, when he received ( I ertns an order from the Genera to gallop forward

and harrass the rear of þÿI aez's retreating army. Morillo had not recognised, at the distance, the fragment which remained of þÿLopez s squadron, which he would never, otherwise, have sent on such a service, especially after the þÿmorning s work. Bash as the order was, it was, of course, obeyed. þÿ On the perfectly level prairie, which was the scene of the operation, what ensued was in view of both armies. Faez, provoked at the j insolence of the little squadron, balled and put himself in person at the head of a splended corps of about 300 men. his guard, the j well known flower of his army, in scarlet j uniforms, and every man superbly mounted ; i and this corps was seen to detach itself from | the main body and rapidly approach the I little hand, whose destruction seemed inevitable before the swoop of that force. Lopez asked his men if they would stand or run. The reply was that they would do as he should. His answer was to fling himself from his horse, and command them to do the same, thus burning his ships, and then to form his men into line, to stand their ground as long as they could with the lances and carabines, which were their arms. He thus repulsed the charge of þÿI aez and his guaro. refusing to surrender, maintaining himself till Alordlo could hasten up alibis cavalry to their support, and till the able þÿI aez, with whom his retreat was of much more importance than the annihilation of this handful of gallant fellows, whom none admired more than he himself, withdrew his guard, and left
Lopez, with what remained of his dismounted squadron, to receive the cordial embraces of his General, and the plaudits of the w hole nrmy, who hod witnessed the scene. To be continued.'

Numbers of them came from distant parts ofthe country; the East Coast of Demerara liberally supplying its tribute to the tide of population,---! hanks to the special Trains rue on that day by the Railway Company for the accommodation of the public Like the natives of most warm countries, where subsistence is easy, the labourer j þÿol thiscolouy are, though rather thought less, of a gay and social turn ; their two great delights being sight-seeing and chattering. A more inquisitive race of people, the Americans not excepted, does not exist. Hence, as they are also t very imitative race of people, they mav be very easily taught. As members of u community, their great fault at þÿpresen is, that they are too easily satisfied with bare existence. The consequence if, that when they have laboured enough to provide for toe wants of nature, they cease to labour because they have no other wants which they think worth the price of exertion. Nowhere, perhaps, would general education bo more advantageous, in a social point of view, than here. That our people would make

great progress in mental cultivation if: evulei-t from what we have said above Rut that cultivation, by creating as if always does, those artificial tastes and fanciful w ants, which are the very germs of commerce, would remove that fault which we now find with our þÿpeople that they work little, because little work in such a country ns this suffices for the supply of the necessary wants of man Ry having other wants than their natural wants to gratify, they would have a motive to work harder and more steadily. The trunk searchers at Liverpool merely glanced at the label, supposing it to be medicine, and passed or So much fur Irish ingenuity.

Glasgow North Daily Mail, November 1. Tnoroti much mischief has we fear, been occasioned by delay, we arc pleased to find that a political movement by the leading men of the Reform party no longer depends on the slender found., tion of newspaper surmise. It is now an actual tact that a meeting of the Council of the Manchester Parliamentary Reform Association was held at that city on Tuesday evening last. It was presided over by Mr. \\ ilson, the experienced and influential chairman of the Anti-Corn- Law League; and was attended by Mr. Bright, Mr. Kershaw, and many other of the foremost men of the district. The utmost unanimity of sentiment prevailed, and the deliberations ended in arraun-c mcnts being made for a great aggregate meeting of Reformers, in the first week in December, for the purpose of securing such a measure of Reform as may be sat isfnetory to t he country at large. We have already expressed our opinion of the mistake which has been committed by waiting until December to consider a measure which will then in all likelihood have been sanctioned by the Cabinet, instead of framing suggestions in September which might have influenced Minsters in their deliberations on the general scope and tendency of the measure. The opinion we then expressed we still entertain ; but " what can't be cured must be endured," and as, like Moses yi the Vicar ot Wakefield, we are unable to deny that " whatever þÿis is," we must be content to take the case as it stands, and endea-

vour to make the best of circumstances as they actually exist. Thedelayismuc.lt to be deplored on all accounts, but lost, time cannot be recalled, atui it will be wiser to look with hopeful hearts to the future, instead of wasting our time m useless lamentations on the irrevocable past. We do not evpect that the intended meeting will exercise any material influence on the character and tendency of the forthcoming Reform Bill. Its chief value will consist in giving efficiency to political movements, which may become necessary after the bill has been laid on the table of the house. The immediate result of the Manchester meeting will likely be the formation of Reform Associations in almost all the large towns in the manufacturing districts. Those associations will have a common ground of action, and without abating a tittle of their local independence, they will look to the parent association at Manchester for

counsel ami support. That should lead to a unity of purpose between the different towns, and, on the occurrence of any emergency, petitions \vill he got. up, meetings convened, and the most effectual means adopted for securing a general and convincing expression of the popular will. Hacked, then, by the powerful manifestations of the popular will, which such a combination would elicit and direct, the Reform leaders in Parliament, in dealing with the Bill which the Government offers to the nation, will speak as those " having authority," and will he aide to command a degree of attention which would not be accorded to their individual opinions. In resisting any proposals they may think proper to make for the extension of the franchise, and on other points, the Minister will feel that he is opposing not merely t lie wishes of a score or two of gentlemen on the benches before him, hut the will of millions of people speaking through their representatives. Thus, although the main features of the Bill may he agreed upon by the Cabinet long before December, and it may have assumed the form in which it will he presented to Parliament, the will of the Minister is not law, as the Bill may he completely i e-moddlcd by the representatives of the people; and it is when amendments are brought forward by the more advanced Liberals that the proposed organization n the manufacturing districts will manifest itself in a peculiar and forcible manner. Reform Associations in the chief

towns and cities of the kingdom cannot fail to have a most beneficial effect. If the Minister retrogrades in the path of Reform, they will impel him onward. It he is timid, they will encourage him. If lie is attacked by the enemies of progress, they will support him. On all accounts, then, we approve of the movement, late though it be, which is just about to commence, it is headed by experienced and popular men, and, under their direction, such a combination of influence will he effected as cannot fail of giving a most powerful aid in securing for the country such a measure of Reform as if. is justly entitled to expect.

The a or king account tor the first six months of the current year, which according to custom of the It oval Mail Steam Packet Company, has been transmitted to each of the Shareholders, will not admit of comparison, as to its various items, with any working account hitherto presented. The change of routes upon the West India line, which took place in \ugnst, 1850, affects both the tec ipts aad disbursements; and in January last, is the Shareholders arc aware, the Company opened an entirely new line of steam communication between the Brazils and the River Plate, of course requiring considerable expenditure in hiring premises, establishing stocks of coal at various de pots, preparing agencies , » all of which ' ion » mooring a a x' v i i ii a , and appointing ever, as wi

U\» <Q & <D 3£ ATI 8« as the receipts, are exhibited in the working account, giving a surplus of £()(),- (>51 8s. 8d. upon the first half of 1851 ; being £21,125 17s. lOd. over the surplus of the corresponding half of the previous year. The Directors are not aware that they can add any further observations respecting the working account, the figures upon which sufficiently testify to tiie steady increase of the Company's prosperity, and to the unquestionably sound position of its affairs. At the same time, however, that the Directors fee! satisfied with the Company's prospects, they are convinced that tliere is always room for improvement, and that it will still he their duty to exert every effort towards affording the most extensive and rapid postal communication, combined with the greatest amount of public accommodation. With this convicsion the five largest class steam ships, now in preparation, were ordered to ho built ; and acting upon the same principle, the Directors finding that their screw steamer, the "Esk," did not accomplish the requisite speed, or offer sufficient passenger accommodation tor the river Plate, a purchase was at once made of the new iron paddlcwheel steamer, the " Prince," of 440 tons builders' admeasurement, with the nominal power of 200 horses, which vessel had made an average speed of 12 knots in one or two experimental voyages ; a rate which can scarcely fail to allord satisfaction between Rio de Janeiro and Buenos Ayres, where she is now stationed. The "Esk" being thus relieved

from duty in the river Plate, has been sent to the West Indies, where she will probably he employed hereafter to improve some branch of service hitherto pany's schooner " Lurtie" having been 0 pei formed by sails alone ; anil the Comyears incessantly employed in a tropical climate, was found to require such extensive repair that, as the most advisable course, she lias been sold by public auction. Since the general meeting of the Shareholders in April last, the five new shins building for the Atlantic service have all been launched, and are now receiving, or preparing to receive, their machinery. As occurs upon all such occasions, causes of delay have arisen beyond the controul of the Directors, hut there is reason to hope that the whole of these ships may be completed in time to commence running between Southampton ai d Chagrcs in the beginning of

this opportunity to reiterate their former assurances that not only these five ships, but the "Prince" also, will be paid tor without the necessity of making anv call upon the Shareholders. The Directors congratulate the Shareholders upon the satisfactory commencement of the Brazil line of communication : as notwithstanding the difficulties inseparably connected with a new enterprise, particularly with foreign nations, all parties have concurred in expressions of high satisfaction at the regularity already exhibited, and the accommodation afforded. þÿ The Directors have not lost sight of the importance which, as was stated in their last report, must in the present state of the communications with the Pacific, he attached to the early completion of the railroad across the Isthmus of Panama ; and of the great interest which this Company has in a safe and expeditious system of transit between the two oceans upon the most favorable terms. To ensure this object the Directors are still ui negotiation with ihe Panama Railroad Company, and are prepared to adopt the same course which has been pursued by those connected with the American Steam Packet Companies, by a loau of money lor such a moderate amount and on such security as may appear eligible.

In order fully to ascertain Ihe expediency of such a loan, the Company's Colonial Superintendent left Southampton by the West India steamer of the 2nd instant for Chagres, and after the in spection of the railroad, with an engi neer, he will proceed to New York to communicate with the Directors of the Panama Railroad Company on the sub ject. Notwithstanding the decision of a select committee of the House of Commons in favor of a steain packet comma mcation with the Australian Colonies via the Cape of Good Hope, it has found so little favor with the mercantile community that the Directors feel convinced the route by the Isthmus of Panama offers superior advantages; and, even without a mail contract, that steam vessels will probably soon he established between Panama and Australia. This would so manifestly tend to benefit the interest of the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company that the Directors will not lail to render every assistance towards the promotion of such an undertaking. The Company's original charter of incorporation contained a clause restricting the conveyance of passengers, specie, and other merchandise, b\ the Company's vessels " to and from such ports and places ami at such times as may he defined in any contract or contracts for the time being in course of fulfilment for the conveyance of the mails." As it was considered this restriction might under certain circumstances he found dotrmental, the Directors submitted the >. ase to the Uueen in council, and Her Ma-

jesty has been pleased to grant a supplemental charter, by which the Company's vessels may now he employed in any branch service, whether with or without mails on hoard, at the discretion of the court of Directors. The same reasons that operated in April last against an immediate increase of tiie rate of dividend apply with nearly equal force at present ; as the Shareholders will readily comprehend the necessity that exists for restoring the reserve and insurance f inds, as a prudent provision p amst casualties and to afford means of encountering competition. With this conviction, therefore, the Directors recommend a dividend for the first half of the current year at the rate of £2 per sham (free of income fax), payable on and from the 14th instant (October.)

True Lloquencc. Clearness, force and eloquence, are the qualities which produce conviction. True eloquence, indeed, does not consist in speech. It caunot be brought from far. Labour mid learning may toil for it, but they may toil in vain. Words and phrases may be muishalled in every way, bui they cannot compass it. It must exist in the man, in the subject, and in the occasion. Affected passion, inlensc expression, the pomp of declamation, all may aspire after it þÿ they cannot reach it. It comes, if it comes at all, like the outbreak ing of a fountain from the earth, or the bursting forth of volcanic fires, with spontaneous, original, native force. The graces taught in the schools, the costly ornaments, and studied contrivances of speech, shock and disgust men, when their own lives and the late of their wives, their childicn, and their country, hang on the decision of the hour. Then, patriotism is eloquent ; then, self devotion is eloquent. The clear conception, outrunning the deductions of logic, the high purpose, the firm resolve, the dauntless spirit, speaking on the tongue, beaming from the eye, informing every feature, and urging the whole man onward, right onward to his subject þÿ this is eloquence; or rather it is something greater and higher than all eloquence, it is action þÿ noble, sublime, goodlike action.
